challenges.title: Alert stack
challenges.brief: Our billing app sends four kinds of message, good news, information, warnings and errors, and I'd like you to build a notifications page that shows them together. Someone glancing at the page should be able to tell immediately which message is good news and which needs action, and each message should offer one clear thing to do next. All the wording is supplied, and the attached reference is exactly the page we want, so match it as closely as you can. Colour alone mustn't carry the meaning, because some of our users can't rely on it, and it has to work with a screen reader. It's done when a user can tell what each message is about and what to do without reading every word.

requirements.text: The page heading reads Notifications, with the line Four messages from the last 24 hours under it
Four banners in this order: success, info, warning, error
Each banner has an icon, a bold title, one line of text and a text button
The banner titles, texts and button labels match the key facts
Each banner is tinted in its own colour family (green, blue, amber, red) with a stronger stripe on its left edge
The icons are drawn shapes that match their kind: a tick, an i, an exclamation mark and a cross
The banners form a single centred column with even gaps between them
The banners are a list and the text buttons are real buttons
Text is easy to read against each banner's tint

keyFacts: Four messages from the last 24 hours
Invoice INV-2041 for $1,280.00 was paid by Northwind Traders.
Version 4.2 adds shared workspaces and faster PDF exports.
You have used 9.1 GB of your 10 GB plan. Uploads pause at the limit.
We could not reach Google Drive. Your last 3 changes are saved on this device.
challenges.content:
Page title: Notifications
Subtitle: Four messages from the last 24 hours
Messages, newest first (kind; title; text; action):
1. Success; Payment received; Invoice INV-2041 for $1,280.00 was paid by Northwind Traders.; View invoice
2. Information; New version available; Version 4.2 adds shared workspaces and faster PDF exports.; See what's new
3. Warning; Storage almost full; You have used 9.1 GB of your 10 GB plan. Uploads pause at the limit.; Upgrade plan
4. Error; Sync failed; We could not reach Google Drive. Your last 3 changes are saved on this device.; Try again
acceptance: I can tell at a glance which message is good news and which needs action
The kind of each message is clear even without colour
Each message offers one clear next step
A screen reader announces each message sensibly
Put side by side with the reference, it is hard to tell them apart
designNotes: calm, roomy single column
soft tints with a stronger left stripe per kind
text in a dark shade of each banner's own colour
small underlined actions at the right

challenges.title: Empty state
challenges.brief: When a new customer opens Lumen for the first time, their projects screen is empty, and at the moment it just looks broken. I'd like you to design the empty state for it. A new customer should understand straight away that nothing is wrong, why projects are useful, and what to do next, with creating a project as the main path and importing as the alternative. Add a small, friendly picture so the page feels welcoming. The text is supplied, and the attached reference shows exactly what we're after: get as close to it as you can. It's done when a first-time customer feels invited, not stuck, and knows exactly which button to press.

requirements.text: The heading reads No projects yet
The sentence under the heading matches the key facts
Two buttons, Create project then Import from Trello, side by side
From top to bottom: illustration, heading, sentence, buttons, all centred on the page
The illustration is drawn inline: a folder in indigo shades with a paper sheet behind its front and a white circle with a plus sign
Create project is a solid indigo button with white text; Import from Trello is white with a thin grey outline
The illustration has a text alternative
The buttons are real buttons and the heading is the page's only main heading

keyFacts: Projects keep your files, tasks and teammates in one place. Create your first one to get started.
challenges.content:
Product: Lumen (team workspace app)
Page: Projects (the account has no projects yet)
Heading: No projects yet
Message: Projects keep your files, tasks and teammates in one place. Create your first one to get started.
Main action: Create project
Second action: Import from Trello
acceptance: A first-time customer can tell that the page is empty on purpose, not broken
Creating a project is clearly the main next step, and importing is the alternative
The page feels friendly and welcoming
Both actions work with a keyboard and have clear names
It matches the reference design closely in structure and look
designNotes: welcoming and uncluttered
everything centred with generous space above
one indigo accent, used for the main action and the illustration
secondary action visibly quieter than the primary

challenges.title: Checkout steps
challenges.brief: Shoppers in our checkout keep asking where they are and how much remains, so I'd like you to build a progress indicator for the payment step, along with the order summary. At a glance a shopper should see which steps they've finished, which step they're on and what's still to come, and they should be able to check what they're paying before moving on. The figures are supplied, and the attached reference is the exact target; I'll judge your page by how closely it matches. Progress mustn't be shown by colour alone, and a screen reader should announce the current step. It's done when a shopper knows where they are and what they owe without thinking.

requirements.text: The page heading reads Checkout
Four steps in this order: Cart, Shipping, Payment, Review
Cart and Shipping are shown done (filled circle with a tick); Payment is current (outlined circle with 3, bold label); Review is upcoming (grey, with 4)
A line joins the circles; it is in the accent colour up to the current step and grey after it
An Order summary card under the steps lists Subtotal (3 items) $184.00, Shipping $9.50, Tax $15.48 and Total $208.98
The total row is bold and separated from the lines above by a rule
A full-width Continue to review button ends the card
The steps are an ordered list in a labelled navigation, and the current step is marked as current for screen readers

challenges.content:
Page: Checkout
Steps, in order: 1 Cart, 2 Shipping, 3 Payment, 4 Review
Completed steps: Cart, Shipping
Current step: Payment (step 3)
Order summary:
- Subtotal (3 items): $184.00
- Shipping: $9.50
- Tax: $15.48
- Total: $208.98
Button: Continue to review
acceptance: I can tell which steps are finished, which one I'm on and what is left
The current step is announced to a screen reader, not shown by colour alone
The order total and how it adds up are easy to check
Moving on to the next step is one obvious action
Next to the reference, nothing important is missing or out of place
designNotes: clean and trustworthy
one indigo accent marks progress and the main action
steps spread evenly across the width of the card
figures right-aligned against their labels

challenges.title: Tabbed panel
challenges.brief: Atlas Logistics needs the Billing page of its account settings. The billing contact comes here to check their plan, when the next payment is due and what they've paid recently, and should be able to move to the other settings sections easily. The details are supplied, and the reference design is exactly what we want; match it closely. The section switcher must work properly with a keyboard and a screen reader. It's done when the billing contact can answer "what do we pay and when?" in a few seconds.

requirements.text: The page heading reads Atlas Logistics, with Account settings for the Business workspace under it
Five tabs in this order: Overview, Billing, Team, Integrations, Security
The selected tab, Billing, is clearly distinguished from the others with colour, weight and an underline
The panel shows a Billing heading and the sentence about renewal from the key facts
Four labelled details in two columns: Plan, Billing contact, Next invoice, Payment method, with the values in the key facts
A Recent invoices table with columns Invoice, Date, Amount, Status and three rows: INV-3108, INV-2987, INV-2861
Amounts are right-aligned and every status reads Paid in green
The details are a description list and the table has header cells
The tabs are buttons in a tab list, with the selected one marked as selected

keyFacts: Account settings for the Business workspace
Your plan renews automatically. Invoices are emailed to the billing contact.

challenges.title: Settings toggles
challenges.brief: Harbor Studio needs its notification settings screen. People come here to switch particular notifications on or off, so they must see the current state of every setting at a glance and change it with one action. Settings are grouped by kind; all of them, and their current states, are supplied. The reference design is the exact target; match it as closely as you can. Every switch must be a real, labelled control that works with a keyboard and a screen reader. It's done when a user can find and change any setting in seconds.

requirements.text: The page heading reads Settings
A left menu with Profile, Account, Notifications, Privacy, Billing in that order, with Notifications highlighted as current
Three groups in this order: Email (3 settings), Push notifications (3 settings), Workspace (2 settings)
Each setting shows its name, helper text and a switch, with the names and helper texts in the key facts
On: Weekly summary, Mentions, Direct messages, Task reminders, Billing alerts. Off: Product updates, Quiet hours, New members
On and off switches are clearly different: accent colour with the knob right versus grey with the knob left
Rows inside a group are separated by thin lines
Each switch is a real checkbox with a visible label, and its helper text is linked to it
The section menu is a list of links in a navigation landmark

keyFacts: A digest of activity across your projects, sent every Monday at 8:00.
News about features and improvements, about once a month.
An email when someone mentions you in a comment.
Notify me when a teammate sends me a message.
Remind me 1 hour before a task is due.
Tell me when someone joins the Harbor Studio workspace.
Warn me 7 days before the card on file is charged.
challenges.content:
Workspace: Harbor Studio
Page: Settings
Settings sections: Profile, Account, Notifications, Privacy, Billing
Current section: Notifications
Notification settings by group (name; description; on or off):
Email
- Weekly summary; A digest of activity across your projects, sent every Monday at 8:00.; on
- Product updates; News about features and improvements, about once a month.; off
- Mentions; An email when someone mentions you in a comment.; on
Push notifications
- Direct messages; Notify me when a teammate sends me a message.; on
- Task reminders; Remind me 1 hour before a task is due.; on
- Quiet hours; Pause push notifications from 22:00 to 07:00.; off
Workspace
- New members; Tell me when someone joins the Harbor Studio workspace.; off
- Billing alerts; Warn me 7 days before the card on file is charged.; on
acceptance: I can tell at a glance which notifications are on and which are off
I can always see which settings section I am in
Every switch has a clear name, so it works with a screen reader and a keyboard
Related settings are easy to find together
It matches the reference design closely in structure and look
designNotes: orderly and easy to scan
narrow menu column, wide content column
white cards with soft borders on an off-white page
indigo marks what is on or current

challenges.title: Comment thread
challenges.brief: Our team discussion tool needs a thread view. Readers should follow the conversation in order, see who said what and when, reply to any comment, and add their own reply at the end. The thread itself is supplied, and the attached reference is exactly what we want, so match it as closely as you can. Keep it calm and readable even when a thread gets long, and make sure the reply box and buttons work with a keyboard and a screen reader. It's done when someone can catch up on the whole discussion in a minute and join in.

requirements.text: The label Growth team sits above the heading Should we switch onboarding emails to a weekly digest?
A 5 comments heading, then five comments by Dana Whitfield, Marcus Lee, Sofia Alvarez, Priya Nair and Tom Okafor in that order
Marcus Lee's and Sofia Alvarez's comments are indented replies to Dana Whitfield's
Each comment has a round avatar with the person's initials, a bold name, a timestamp, the text and a Reply action
Each person's avatar has its own colour, and the initials are white
The timestamps and comment texts match the key facts
A reply box at the end with the label Write a reply, a text area and a Post reply button
Comments are nested lists, timestamps use time elements, and the text area has a label

keyFacts: Should we switch onboarding emails to a weekly digest?
New sign-ups get six emails in their first week. Unsubscribes doubled since March. I'd like to try one digest on day 7 instead.
Agreed on volume, but the day 1 setup email drives most activations. Can we keep that one?
Keeping day 1 makes sense. I can have the digest template ready by Thursday.
Let's run it as an A/B test on 20% of new accounts for two weeks before we switch everyone.
I'll set up the test cohort in the email tool today and share the dashboard link here.
challenges.content:
Team: Growth team
Discussion title: Should we switch onboarding emails to a weekly digest?
Comment count: 5 comments

2. Marcus Lee; ML; 1 hour ago; Agreed on volume, but the day 1 setup email drives most activations. Can we keep that one?
3. Sofia Alvarez; SA; 45 minutes ago; Keeping day 1 makes sense. I can have the digest template ready by Thursday.
4. Priya Nair; PN; 30 minutes ago; Let's run it as an A/B test on 20% of new accounts for two weeks before we switch everyone.

Action on each comment: Reply
New reply: placeholder: Write a reply; button: Post reply
acceptance: I can follow the conversation in order and see who said what and when
Each comment's author is easy to recognise
Replying is easy to find, both per comment and at the end
The reply box has a clear name for screen readers
Next to the reference, nothing important is missing or out of place
designNotes: friendly but focused
one narrow centred column
comments as rounded white cards with soft borders
colour only in the avatars and the indigo actions

The table has header cells, the sorted column is announced as sorted, and the search field has a label
The pagination is a labelled navigation with the current page marked

challenges.title: Modal over page
challenges.brief: In Fieldnote, deleting a project opens a confirmation dialog over the projects page, and we want that moment captured. The user must understand exactly what will be lost and that it can't be undone, and cancelling should feel safe. Content is supplied; the reference design is exactly what we want, so match it closely. The dialog must be accessible. Done means nobody deletes a project by accident.

requirements.text: A top bar with Fieldnote on the left and Projects, Reports, Settings links on the right
Behind the overlay: a Projects heading and three cards in a row: Spring campaign (48 files), Customer interviews (31 files), Brand refresh (22 files), each with its description
The whole page is dimmed by a half-transparent black overlay that covers the full window
A white dialog is centred on the window, above the overlay, with rounded corners and a shadow
The dialog is titled Delete project and its warning text matches the key facts
Two fields in this order: Type the project name to confirm (empty, hinting Spring campaign) and Reason for deleting (filled with Campaign has ended)
An unticked checkbox labelled Also delete the 12 linked reports
Cancel then Delete project at the bottom right; Delete project is solid red with white text, Cancel is outlined
The dialog is marked as a modal dialog and named by its title
Every field and the checkbox has a visible label

keyFacts: Launch plan, ad copy and landing pages for the April release.
Notes and recordings from 14 interviews with clinic managers.
Logo options, colour studies and the updated style guide.
This permanently removes Spring campaign and its 48 files. It cannot be undone.
Type the project name to confirm
challenges.content:
Product: Fieldnote
Navigation: Projects, Reports, Settings (current: Projects)
Projects (name; description; file count):
- Spring campaign; Launch plan, ad copy and landing pages for the April release.; 48 files
- Customer interviews; Notes and recordings from 14 interviews with clinic managers.; 31 files
- Brand refresh; Logo options, colour studies and the updated style guide.; 22 files
Open dialog: deleting the project Spring campaign
- Title: Delete project
- Warning: This permanently removes Spring campaign and its 48 files. It cannot be undone.
- Field: Type the project name to confirm; placeholder: Spring campaign
- Field: Reason for deleting; filled in: Campaign has ended
- Checkbox: Also delete the 12 linked reports
- Buttons: Cancel; Delete project (the destructive action)
acceptance: It is clear what will be deleted and that it cannot be undone
The destructive action is clearly distinct from cancelling
The page behind is visible but clearly inactive
The dialog and its fields are accessible to keyboard and screen reader users
It matches the reference design closely in structure and look
designNotes: serious without being alarming
the page behind stays recognisable through the dim
red used only for the destructive button
dialog compact and focused, about a third of the window wide
